mediaItem.network: Lava for Good Podcasts, Signal Company No. 1
mediaItem.seriesType: Episodic Series (each episode is generally a standalone story)
mediaItem.focusTheme_Work: Wrongful convictions, investigative journalism, police and prosecutorial misconduct, eyewitness misidentification, personal narratives of exonerees.
mediaItem.keyStats:
-   Two separate murders in the Bronx, Jan 1995 (Denise Raymond, Bath Diop).
-   Seven people initially charged in connection with one or both murders.
-   Six individuals wrongfully convicted.
-   Convictions heavily reliant on testimony from one primary witness (Miriam Tavares) and her teenage translator (Kathy Gomez).
-   Two members of the Sex Money Murder gang confessed to the Diop murder in 2003, nine years before this information led to the exonerations.
-   NYPD failed to connect the 2003 confessions to the existing convictions due to record-keeping errors.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode details the wrongful conviction of Eric Glissen and five others for two separate 1995 Bronx murders they did not commit. Relying on shaky eyewitness testimony from Miriam Tavares and her young translator Kathy Gomez, police linked the unrelated murders of FedEx executive Denise Raymond and cab driver Bath Diop. Glissen was convicted for the Diop murder and sentenced to 25-to-life, ultimately serving over 17 years. While incarcerated, Glissen's persistent investigation uncovered phone records from Diop's stolen phone implicating members of the Sex Money Murder gang. This information reached US Attorney investigator John O'Malley, who realized two gang members had confessed to the Diop murder years prior in 2003, a fact missed due to an NYPD error stating the crime didn't exist in their records. This revelation led to Glissen's release in 2012 and the eventual exoneration of all six individuals.

featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: Released approx. 5-6 months after Eric Glissen (Spring 2013), exoneration followed.
contributingFactorsRaw: Eyewitness misidentification (Tavares added her implication late), Questionable voice identification process, Police misconduct (Donnelly failing to verify if she actually called the cab service), Tunnel vision.
organizationsInvolvedRaw: (Same as Glissen, implicated in the group exoneration process).
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Bath Diop murder (see Glissen entry). Watkins was accused of being involved based on a theory she called the cab, which was later found to be untrue.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Testimony of Miriam Tavares (claiming Watkins was present, urging others on); Cab dispatcher voice identification (conducted under questionable circumstances).
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Not detailed. Key defense point would be lack of connection to others and the unverified claim she called the cab.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Same as Eric Glissen, primarily the discovery of the actual perpetrators' confessions. The fact she didn't call the cab service was also noted as discovered later, though timing relative to exoneration isn't specified.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Gilbert Vega and Joey Rodriguez (for the Diop murder).

keyQuotesRaw: Eric Glissen during interrogation: "I don't know what you're talking about. I have no idea. I didn't do anything. I just want to go home and see my daughter."
Eric Glissen on survival: "I died on my feet, not on my knees... Every problem has an expiration date."
Eric Glissen on empowering his daughters: "On their room doors, I wrote in big letters, girls can do anything."
Investigator John O'Malley upon reading Glissen's letter: "Holy shit... a cab driver, sound view section of the Bronx 1995. I knew who did that."
Dan Slepian on systemic issues: "...a system that is so pathological and irrational."
Dan Slepian on solutions: "What is our true genuine safeguard against injustice? And the answer is educating people..."
Eric Glissen on prison system: "Prisons in America is really a for profit entity... the prosecutor's budgets got bigger."
systemicIssuesRaw: Reliance on unreliable eyewitness testimony (especially single witness).
Police tunnel vision and confirmation bias.
Coercion and manipulation of witnesses (especially vulnerable ones like minors).
Failure to conduct thorough investigations (e.g., checking witness vantage points, verifying phone logs).
Mishandling or loss of physical evidence by prosecution.
Lack of communication and information sharing between different law enforcement agencies (NYPD and US Attorney's Office).
Prosecutorial resistance to admitting error and delaying exonerations.
Impact of poverty on obtaining adequate legal defense.
Profit motive within the prison-industrial complex.
Decline of vocational and educational programs in prisons.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Implement reforms for eyewitness identification procedures.
Increase accountability for police and prosecutorial misconduct (revisiting immunity).
Mandate improved information sharing between agencies.
Establish/strengthen conviction integrity units within DA offices.
Promote public education about wrongful conviction causes (jury awareness).
Reinstate and fund robust vocational and educational programs in prisons to aid rehabilitation and reduce recidivism.
Address the financial incentives within the justice and prison systems.
personalNarrativeRaw: Eric Glissen described the profound trauma of being arrested just after his daughter's birth, feeling his life crumble. He emphasized his unwavering belief in his innocence and relentless fight from prison, utilizing the law library and writing countless letters. He found strength in support networks like RTA and fellow innocent inmates. Post-exoneration, he dedicates himself to advocacy, stressing the importance of inner strength, positivity, and holding onto hope. His final thoughts focus critically on the prison system's profit motives and the detrimental removal of rehabilitative programs, arguing for systemic change and accountability.
